---
title: "VAR analysis"
subtitle: "Industrial production and University of Michigan consumer sentiment"
---

```{r}
#| label: setup
source("R/setup.R")

suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(tseries)  # adf.test
  library(urca)     # ur.kpss, ca.jo
  library(vars)     # VARselect, VAR, causality, irf, fevd
})

umc_ts <- read_monthly_ts("data/umcsent.csv")

fmt_p <- function(p) {
  if (p < 2.2e-16) return("< 2.2e-16")
  if (p < 0.001) return(paste("=", format(p, digits = 3, scientific = TRUE)))
  paste("=", sprintf("%.4f", p))
}

# Johansen test statistics next to their critical values
johansen_table <- function(jo) {
  data.frame(
    Hypothesis = rownames(jo@cval),
    Statistic = round(jo@teststat, 2),
    jo@cval,
    check.names = FALSE,
    row.names = NULL
  )
}
```

The second series is the University of Michigan Index of Consumer Sentiment
(UMCSENT), a monthly survey of how US households see current and future
economic conditions. The question is whether consumer sentiment carries
information about future industrial production.

## Consumer sentiment

```{r}
#| label: fig-umcsent
#| fig-cap: "University of Michigan consumer sentiment (1966:Q1 = 100)"
autoplot(umc_ts) +
  labs(x = "Year", y = "Index (1966:Q1 = 100)")
```

Unlike industrial production, sentiment has no clear upward trend but large
cyclical swings. It falls in the 2001 recession, the 2008–2009 financial crisis
and the 2020 pandemic; its lowest value in the sample is `r min(umc_ts)`
(`r format(zoo::as.yearmon(time(umc_ts)[which.min(umc_ts)]))`).

## Stationarity of UMCSENT

```{r}
#| label: tbl-umc-tests
#| tbl-cap: "KPSS statistics and ADF p-values, UMCSENT in levels"
umc_kpss <- sapply(c(tau = "tau", mu = "mu"), function(type) ur.kpss(umc_ts, type = type)@teststat)

adf_lags <- c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 12, 24)
umc_adf <- data.frame(
  Lag = adf_lags,
  `ADF p-value` = sapply(adf_lags, function(k) suppressWarnings(adf.test(umc_ts, k = k)$p.value)),
  check.names = FALSE
)
umc_pp <- PP.test(umc_ts)

umc_adf
```

1. The KPSS statistics (`r round(umc_kpss["tau"], 4)` with trend and
   `r round(umc_kpss["mu"], 4)` with a constant) are above the 5% critical
   values (0.146 and 0.463), so stationarity in levels is rejected.
2. All ADF p-values are above 0.05 and the Phillips-Perron test gives
   p `r fmt_p(umc_pp$p.value)`, so the unit root cannot be rejected.

All three tests agree: UMCSENT is not stationary in levels.

## Cointegration (Johansen test)

Industrial production is not seasonally adjusted, so both the cointegration
test and the VAR include **monthly (seasonal) dummy variables**
(`season = 12`). Without them, the seasonal pattern ends up in the residuals
and distorts the tests. The lag order of the levels VAR used by the Johansen
test is chosen with the Akaike information criterion (AIC).

```{r}
#| label: johansen
dset <- cbind(ip_ts, umc_ts)
colnames(dset) <- c("IPB", "UMCSENT")

lag_select <- VARselect(dset, lag.max = 12, type = "const", season = 12)
lag_select$selection
johansen_k <- unname(lag_select$selection["AIC(n)"])

johansen_trace <- ca.jo(dset, type = "trace", ecdet = "const", K = johansen_k, season = 12)
johansen_eigen <- ca.jo(dset, type = "eigen", ecdet = "const", K = johansen_k, season = 12)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-johansen
#| tbl-cap: "Johansen test: trace (top) and maximum eigenvalue (bottom)"
jo_trace <- johansen_table(johansen_trace)
jo_eigen <- johansen_table(johansen_eigen)
jo_trace
jo_eigen
```

With K = `r johansen_k` lags, for r = 0 both the trace statistic (`r jo_trace$Statistic[2]`) and the maximum
eigenvalue statistic (`r jo_eigen$Statistic[2]`) are below their 5% critical
values (`r jo_trace[["5pct"]][2]` and `r jo_eigen[["5pct"]][2]`). The null
hypothesis r = 0 cannot be rejected: there is no cointegrating relationship, so
no stable long-run link between industrial production and consumer sentiment.
A VECM is therefore not estimated; instead, a VAR is fitted to the first
differences of both series to make them stationary.

## First differences

```{r}
#| label: tbl-diff-tests
#| tbl-cap: "ADF and Phillips-Perron p-values for the differenced series"
dset_diff <- data.frame(
  IPB_d = diff(as.numeric(ip_ts)),
  UMCSENT_d = diff(as.numeric(umc_ts))
)

diff_tests <- data.frame(
  Series = names(dset_diff),
  `ADF p-value` = sapply(dset_diff, function(x) suppressWarnings(adf.test(x)$p.value)),
  `PP p-value` = sapply(dset_diff, function(x) PP.test(x)$p.value),
  check.names = FALSE,
  row.names = NULL
)
diff_tests
```

For both differenced series the ADF and Phillips-Perron p-values are 0.01
(below 0.05), so the unit root is rejected: both series are stationary after
differencing and can be used in the VAR.

## VAR lag selection and estimation

The VAR is estimated on the first differences with a constant and monthly
dummies. The lag order should leave residuals free of autocorrelation;
otherwise the Granger tests and the impulse response bands are not reliable.
The table below shows the Portmanteau test for every lag order from 1 to 12.

```{r}
#| label: var
var_lag <- VARselect(dset_diff, lag.max = 12, type = "const", season = 12)
var_lag$selection
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-var-lags
#| tbl-cap: "Portmanteau test (20 lags) on the VAR residuals, by lag order"
lag_check <- data.frame(
  `Lag order` = 1:12,
  `Portmanteau p-value` = sapply(1:12, function(p) {
    v <- VAR(dset_diff, p = p, type = "const", season = 12)
    serial.test(v, lags.pt = 20, type = "PT.asymptotic")$serial$p.value
  }),
  check.names = FALSE
)
lag_check[["Portmanteau p-value"]] <- round(lag_check[["Portmanteau p-value"]], 4)
lag_check

var_p <- unname(var_lag$selection["AIC(n)"])
var_model <- VAR(dset_diff, p = var_p, type = "const", season = 12)
```

The Schwarz and Hannan-Quinn criteria choose `r var_lag$selection["SC(n)"]`
lags, but with fewer than 12 lags the residuals remain autocorrelated at the 5%
level. The AIC choice, p = `r var_p`, removes the autocorrelation and is used
below. Twelve lags of monthly data cover one full year, which is plausible for a
non-seasonally adjusted series.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-var-ipb
#| tbl-cap: "Equation for the change in industrial production (IPB_d): lags of UMCSENT_d"
var_summary <- summary(var_model)
ipb_eq <- var_summary$varresult$IPB_d$coefficients
umc_eq <- var_summary$varresult$UMCSENT_d$coefficients
as.data.frame(round(ipb_eq[grep("^UMCSENT_d", rownames(ipb_eq)), ], 4))
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-var-umc
#| tbl-cap: "Equation for the change in consumer sentiment (UMCSENT_d): lags of IPB_d"
umc_on_ipb <- umc_eq[grep("^IPB_d", rownames(umc_eq)), ]
n_sig_ipb_lags <- sum(umc_on_ipb[, "Pr(>|t|)"] < 0.05)
as.data.frame(round(umc_on_ipb, 4))
```

1. In the industrial production equation, sentiment one month earlier
   (`UMCSENT_d.l1`) has a positive coefficient
   (`r round(ipb_eq["UMCSENT_d.l1", "Estimate"], 3)`) that is highly significant
   (p `r fmt_p(ipb_eq["UMCSENT_d.l1", "Pr(>|t|)"])`): an improvement in consumer
   confidence is followed by higher industrial production the next month.
2. In the sentiment equation, only `r n_sig_ipb_lags` of the `r var_p` lags of
   industrial production `r if (n_sig_ipb_lags == 1) "is" else "are"`
   significant at 5%, about what chance alone would produce.

## VAR diagnostics

```{r}
#| label: var-diagnostics
var_serial <- serial.test(var_model, lags.pt = 20, type = "PT.asymptotic")
var_arch <- vars::arch.test(var_model, lags.multi = 12, multivariate.only = TRUE)
var_norm <- normality.test(var_model, multivariate.only = TRUE)

diag_p <- c(
  var_serial$serial$p.value,
  var_arch$arch.mul$p.value,
  var_norm$jb.mul$JB$p.value
)
data.frame(
  Test = c("Portmanteau (autocorrelation, 20 lags)", "Multivariate ARCH (12 lags)", "Jarque-Bera (normality)"),
  `p-value` = sub("^= ", "", sapply(diag_p, fmt_p)),
  check.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-cusum
#| fig-cap: "OLS-CUSUM stability test for each VAR equation"
#| fig-height: 6
stability_model <- stability(var_model, type = "OLS-CUSUM")
plot(stability_model)
```

1. **Autocorrelation:** the Portmanteau test gives
   p `r fmt_p(var_serial$serial$p.value)`, so the residuals show no remaining
   autocorrelation.
2. **ARCH effects and non-normality:** both tests give p < 0.05. The residual
   variance changes over time and the distribution has heavy tails, reflecting
   the 2008–2009 and 2020 shocks. The coefficient estimates remain consistent,
   but standard errors and p-values rely on large-sample approximations and
   should be read with some caution.
3. **Stability:** in the OLS-CUSUM plot, the empirical fluctuation process stays
   within the critical bands for both equations, so there is no evidence of a
   structural break in the parameters. This is a separate property: it does not
   compensate for the ARCH effects above.

## Granger causality

```{r}
#| label: tbl-granger
#| tbl-cap: "Granger causality tests (F-tests on all lags of the causing variable)"
granger_ipb <- causality(var_model, cause = "IPB_d")
granger_umc <- causality(var_model, cause = "UMCSENT_d")

data.frame(
  Direction = c("IPB_d -> UMCSENT_d", "UMCSENT_d -> IPB_d"),
  `F statistic` = round(c(granger_ipb$Granger$statistic, granger_umc$Granger$statistic), 4),
  `p-value` = round(c(granger_ipb$Granger$p.value, granger_umc$Granger$p.value), 4),
  check.names = FALSE
)
```

1. IPB_d → UMCSENT_d: p `r fmt_p(granger_ipb$Granger$p.value)` (> 0.05); changes
   in industrial production do not help predict consumer sentiment.
2. UMCSENT_d → IPB_d: the joint p-value for the `r var_p` lags is
   `r round(granger_umc$Granger$p.value, 4)` (< 0.05), so the null hypothesis of
   no Granger causality is rejected: past changes in consumer sentiment help
   predict changes in industrial production.

The relationship is one-directional: sentiment helps to predict industrial
production, but not the other way round. Granger causality is about
predictive content, not about economic causation.

::: {.callout-note}
In an earlier version of this analysis, the VAR had 4 lags and no seasonal
dummies; its residuals were autocorrelated and the Granger test for
UMCSENT_d → IPB_d was not significant (p = 0.18). Accounting for seasonality
and choosing the lag order so that the residuals are clean changes this result.
:::

## Impulse response functions

```{r}
#| label: fig-irf-umc
#| fig-cap: "Response of IPB_d to a shock in UMCSENT_d (90% bootstrap bands)"
set.seed(123)  # bootstrap confidence bands
irf_umc_to_ipb <- irf(
  var_model,
  impulse = "UMCSENT_d",
  response = "IPB_d",
  n.ahead = 20,
  boot = TRUE,
  ci = 0.90
)
plot(irf_umc_to_ipb, main = "Shock to UMCSENT_d, response of IPB_d")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-irf-ipb
#| fig-cap: "Response of UMCSENT_d to a shock in IPB_d (90% bootstrap bands)"
irf_ipb_to_umc <- irf(
  var_model,
  impulse = "IPB_d",
  response = "UMCSENT_d",
  n.ahead = 20,
  boot = TRUE,
  ci = 0.90
)
plot(irf_ipb_to_umc, main = "Shock to IPB_d, response of UMCSENT_d")
```

```{r}
#| label: irf-significance
# Horizons (months after the shock) at which the 90% band excludes zero
significant_horizons <- function(x, impulse) {
  which(x$Lower[[impulse]][, 1] > 0 | x$Upper[[impulse]][, 1] < 0) - 1
}
and_list <- function(x) {
  if (length(x) == 0) return("at no horizon")
  if (length(x) == 1) return(as.character(x))
  paste(paste(head(x, -1), collapse = ", "), "and", tail(x, 1))
}
sig_umc_to_ipb <- significant_horizons(irf_umc_to_ipb, "UMCSENT_d")
sig_ipb_to_umc <- significant_horizons(irf_ipb_to_umc, "IPB_d")
```

1. A positive shock to consumer sentiment raises industrial production one
   month later (response of
   `r round(irf_umc_to_ipb$irf$UMCSENT_d[2, 1], 2)` index points, with the
   bootstrap band entirely above zero). Over the 20 months shown, the band
   excludes zero only `r and_list(sig_umc_to_ipb)` months after the shock, so
   the effect is concentrated in the first month and is short-lived.
2. For a shock to industrial production, the band excludes zero only
   `r and_list(sig_ipb_to_umc)` months after the shock: production shocks have
   essentially no effect on consumer confidence.

With 90% bands, about 2 of 20 horizons are expected to exclude zero by chance
alone, so isolated significant points far from the shock should not be
over-interpreted.

### Robustness: variable ordering and cumulative effect

The impulse responses above are *orthogonalised* with a Cholesky
decomposition, which requires an ordering of the variables. With industrial
production first, a sentiment shock cannot move production in the same month
by construction. Below, the VAR is re-estimated with sentiment first, and the
**cumulative** responses are computed: since the VAR is in first differences,
the cumulative response of `IPB_d` is the effect on the *level* of the index.

```{r}
#| label: irf-robustness
var_model_rev <- VAR(dset_diff[, c("UMCSENT_d", "IPB_d")], p = var_p, type = "const", season = 12)

set.seed(123)
irf_rev <- irf(var_model_rev, impulse = "UMCSENT_d", response = "IPB_d",
               n.ahead = 12, boot = TRUE, ci = 0.90)

cumulative_irf <- function(model) {
  set.seed(123)
  irf(model, impulse = "UMCSENT_d", response = "IPB_d",
      n.ahead = 12, boot = TRUE, ci = 0.90, cumulative = TRUE)
}
cum_base <- cumulative_irf(var_model)
cum_rev <- cumulative_irf(var_model_rev)

# Size of a one-standard-deviation orthogonal sentiment shock, in index points
shock_size <- function(model, var) {
  chol_factor <- t(chol(summary(model)$covres))
  chol_factor[var, var]
}
resid_corr <- summary(var_model)$corres["IPB_d", "UMCSENT_d"]
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-irf-robustness
#| tbl-cap: "Response of industrial production to a sentiment shock under both orderings (90% bootstrap bands)"
irf_row <- function(x, step, label, ordering) {
  data.frame(
    Ordering = ordering,
    Measure = label,
    Response = round(x$irf$UMCSENT_d[step + 1, 1], 3),
    `Lower 90%` = round(x$Lower$UMCSENT_d[step + 1, 1], 3),
    `Upper 90%` = round(x$Upper$UMCSENT_d[step + 1, 1], 3),
    check.names = FALSE,
    row.names = NULL
  )
}
rbind(
  irf_row(irf_umc_to_ipb, 0, "Same month", "Production first"),
  irf_row(irf_umc_to_ipb, 1, "After 1 month", "Production first"),
  irf_row(cum_base, 12, "Cumulative, 12 months", "Production first"),
  irf_row(irf_rev, 0, "Same month", "Sentiment first"),
  irf_row(irf_rev, 1, "After 1 month", "Sentiment first"),
  irf_row(cum_rev, 12, "Cumulative, 12 months", "Sentiment first")
)
```

1. The residuals of the two equations are only weakly correlated
   (correlation `r round(resid_corr, 2)`), so the ordering matters little.
   With sentiment first, the same-month response is
   `r round(irf_rev$irf$UMCSENT_d[1, 1], 2)` and its band includes zero; the
   response after one month
   (`r round(irf_rev$irf$UMCSENT_d[2, 1], 2)`) remains significant.
2. A one-standard-deviation sentiment shock (about
   `r round(shock_size(var_model, "UMCSENT_d"), 1)` index points of sentiment)
   raises the **level** of industrial production by
   `r round(cum_base$irf$UMCSENT_d[13, 1], 2)` index points after 12 months
   (90% band `r round(cum_base$Lower$UMCSENT_d[13, 1], 2)` to
   `r round(cum_base$Upper$UMCSENT_d[13, 1], 2)`), or
   `r round(cum_rev$irf$UMCSENT_d[13, 1], 2)` with sentiment ordered first. The
   effect is statistically significant but economically small: the index is
   around 100, so this is roughly half a percent.

This supports the view of sentiment indicators as leading indicators of real
industrial activity.

## Forecast error variance decomposition

```{r}
#| label: fig-fevd
#| fig-cap: "Forecast error variance decomposition (10 months)"
#| fig-height: 6
fevd_result <- fevd(var_model, n.ahead = 10)
plot(fevd_result)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-fevd
#| tbl-cap: "Share of forecast error variance at a 10-month horizon"
fevd_10 <- rbind(
  IPB_d = fevd_result$IPB_d[10, ],
  UMCSENT_d = fevd_result$UMCSENT_d[10, ]
)
as.data.frame(round(100 * fevd_10, 2))
```

1. In the first month, almost 100% of the variance of each variable is
   explained by its own shocks.
2. At a 10-month horizon, changes in consumer sentiment explain about
   `r round(100 * fevd_10["IPB_d", "UMCSENT_d"], 2)`% of the forecast error
   variance of industrial production.
3. In the other direction, industrial production explains only
   `r round(100 * fevd_10["UMCSENT_d", "IPB_d"], 2)`% of the variance of
   consumer sentiment.

The decomposition supports a one-sided relationship: sentiment explains a
modest share of the forecast uncertainty of industrial production, while the
reverse share is negligible.

## Does sentiment improve forecasts out of sample?

The Granger test uses the whole sample. A stricter, practical question is
whether sentiment improves **real forecasts**. The VAR is compared with:

- an **AR(12) model** for the change in industrial production with the same
  constant and monthly dummies, i.e. the VAR equation for `IPB_d` *without*
  the lags of sentiment. The only difference between the two models is the
  information in consumer sentiment;
- the **SARIMA** model from the [univariate analysis](univariate.qmd),
  ARIMA(3,1,0)(0,1,1)[12] on log data.

As in the univariate rolling-origin evaluation, every month from June 2016 to
March 2025 the three models are re-estimated on the data available up to that
month and forecast industrial production 1 to 12 months ahead. Forecasts of
monthly changes are added up to give index levels.

```{r}
#| label: var-rolling-cv
n_obs <- length(ip_ts)
n_train <- floor(0.75 * n_obs)  # same split as the univariate analysis (June 2016)
max_h <- 12

ip_values <- as.numeric(ip_ts)
ip_diff <- ts(diff(ip_values), start = c(1990, 2), frequency = 12)
umc_diff <- diff(as.numeric(umc_ts))

oos_errors <- list(
  VAR = matrix(NA, n_obs, max_h),
  `AR(12), no sentiment` = matrix(NA, n_obs, max_h),
  SARIMA = matrix(NA, n_obs, max_h)
)

for (t in n_train:(n_obs - 1)) {
  m <- t - 1                        # differences available at origin t
  steps <- 1:min(max_h, n_obs - t)  # horizons with an observed outcome
  actual <- ip_values[t + steps]

  # VAR with sentiment
  v <- VAR(data.frame(IPB_d = ip_diff[1:m], UMCSENT_d = umc_diff[1:m]),
           p = var_p, type = "const", season = 12)
  fc_var <- predict(v, n.ahead = max_h)$fcst$IPB_d[, "fcst"]

  # Same equation without sentiment; CSS gives least-squares estimates like the VAR
  x <- window(ip_diff, end = time(ip_diff)[m])
  ar <- Arima(x, order = c(var_p, 0, 0), xreg = seasonaldummy(x), method = "CSS")
  fc_ar <- forecast(ar, h = max_h, xreg = seasonaldummy(x, h = max_h))$mean

  # SARIMA on log data (median forecast)
  s <- Arima(ts(ip_values[1:t], start = c(1990, 1), frequency = 12),
             order = c(3, 1, 0), seasonal = c(0, 1, 1), lambda = 0)
  fc_sarima <- forecast(s, h = max_h)$mean

  oos_errors$VAR[t, steps] <- actual - (ip_values[t] + cumsum(fc_var))[steps]
  oos_errors$`AR(12), no sentiment`[t, steps] <- actual - (ip_values[t] + cumsum(as.numeric(fc_ar)))[steps]
  oos_errors$SARIMA[t, steps] <- actual - as.numeric(fc_sarima)[steps]
}

oos_rmse <- function(E, k) sqrt(mean(E[, k]^2, na.rm = TRUE))
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-var-oos
#| tbl-cap: "Rolling-origin RMSE (index points), June 2016 to April 2025"
oos_table <- data.frame(
  Model = names(oos_errors),
  `1 month` = sapply(oos_errors, oos_rmse, k = 1),
  `3 months` = sapply(oos_errors, oos_rmse, k = 3),
  `6 months` = sapply(oos_errors, oos_rmse, k = 6),
  `12 months` = sapply(oos_errors, oos_rmse, k = 12),
  check.names = FALSE,
  row.names = NULL
)
oos_table[, -1] <- round(oos_table[, -1], 3)
oos_table
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-var-dm
#| tbl-cap: "Diebold-Mariano tests on rolling-origin errors"
oos_dm <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c(1, max_h), function(k) {
  do.call(rbind, lapply(c("AR(12), no sentiment", "SARIMA"), function(other) {
    a <- oos_errors$VAR[, k]
    b <- oos_errors[[other]][, k]
    ok <- !is.na(a) & !is.na(b)
    test <- dm.test(a[ok], b[ok], alternative = "two.sided", h = k, power = 2)
    data.frame(
      Horizon = paste(k, if (k == 1) "month" else "months"),
      Comparison = paste("VAR vs", other),
      `DM statistic` = round(unname(test$statistic), 3),
      `p-value` = round(test$p.value, 3),
      check.names = FALSE,
      row.names = NULL
    )
  }))
}))
rownames(oos_dm) <- NULL
oos_dm

dm_var_ar <- function(horizon) {
  oos_dm[["p-value"]][oos_dm$Horizon == horizon & oos_dm$Comparison == "VAR vs AR(12), no sentiment"]
}
```

1. **Adding sentiment does not improve the forecasts.** One month ahead the VAR
   and the AR model without sentiment have practically the same RMSE
   (`r sprintf("%.2f", oos_table[1, "1 month"])` and
   `r sprintf("%.2f", oos_table[2, "1 month"])`; Diebold-Mariano
   p = `r sprintf("%.2f", dm_var_ar("1 month"))`). Twelve months ahead the VAR is
   slightly worse (`r sprintf("%.2f", oos_table[1, "12 months"])` against
   `r sprintf("%.2f", oos_table[2, "12 months"])`), but the difference is not
   significant (p = `r sprintf("%.2f", dm_var_ar("12 months"))`).
2. The VAR is not more accurate than SARIMA at any of the horizons shown; at 1
   and 12 months the differences are not statistically significant.

Sentiment is a statistically significant predictor *in sample* (Granger test),
but this does not translate into better *out-of-sample* forecasts. A likely
reason is that estimating 12 extra sentiment coefficients adds noise that
offsets the small amount of information they carry. This is a common result in macroeconomic
forecasting: in-sample significance is a weak guide to forecasting value.

The comparison uses the latest revised data, not the data that were available
in real time at each forecast origin.

## VAR forecast

```{r}
#| label: fig-var-forecast
#| fig-cap: "VAR forecast of industrial production, 24 months ahead (dashed line = end of data)"
var_forecast <- predict(var_model, n.ahead = 24, ci = 0.90)

fc_ipb_diff <- var_forecast$fcst$IPB_d[, "fcst"]

# Rebuild index levels by adding the forecast changes to the last observed value
last_ipb <- tail(as.numeric(ip_ts), 1)
fc_ipb_level <- cumsum(c(last_ipb, fc_ipb_diff))[-1]

history_time <- as.numeric(time(ip_ts))
last_time_point <- tail(history_time, 1)
forecast_time <- seq(last_time_point + 1 / 12, by = 1 / 12, length.out = length(fc_ipb_level))

df_ipb <- data.frame(
  time = c(history_time, forecast_time),
  value = c(as.numeric(ip_ts), fc_ipb_level)
)

ggplot(df_ipb, aes(x = time, y = value)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = last_time_point, linetype = "dashed", colour = "red") +
  labs(x = "Year", y = "Index (2017 = 100)")
```

1. `predict()` forecasts the next 24 months with a 90% interval.
2. Because the VAR is estimated on differences, the forecasts are monthly
   changes.
3. They are converted back to index levels with `cumsum()`, adding the forecast
   changes to the last observed value (`r round(last_ipb, 2)`).
4. To the right of the dashed red line, the forecast reproduces the seasonal
   pattern through the monthly dummies. On average it stays around
   `r round(mean(fc_ipb_level), 1)` index points over the 24 months and ends at
   `r round(tail(fc_ipb_level, 1), 2)`, close to the recent level of the series.
